common_name: Pescadero Red Garlic (Fisherman's Garlic, Mild Coastal Creole Type)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep, in October-November in zone 9; Pescadero Red is a Creole-type garlic that needs little winter chill to bulb properly, making it far more reliable than hardneck types in mild-winter climates.

directions: Pescadero Red, also called Fisherman's Garlic for its coastal California origins near Pescadero, is a Creole-type softneck garlic grown for its symmetrical bulbs wrapped in brilliant burgundy-streaked skins and a mild, mellow garlic flavor with far less bite than typical hardneck varieties. It is an unusually vigorous grower for a Creole, often producing bulbs larger than its relatives, with 8-12 plump cloves arranged in the tight circular pattern characteristic of the group. Because it needs minimal cold exposure to form bulbs, it thrives in the same mild Gulf South and coastal winters where northern Rocambole and Porcelain garlics routinely fail. Harvest in early summer when the lower leaves brown and 4-5 green leaves remain, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks; well-cured bulbs store from early summer through winter into mid-spring.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm — Pescadero Red variety notes
Gourmet Garlic Gardens — Creole garlic variety descriptions

common_name: Truhart Perfection Pimiento Pepper (Classic Georgia Canning Pimiento)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; Truhart Perfection was released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1943 through pedigree selection out of the older Perfection pimiento for a higher percentage of uniform, heart-shaped, thick-walled fruit, and it became the standard variety of the American pimiento canning industry for decades.

directions: Truhart Perfection traces to a single outstanding plant selected from the original 1913 Perfection pimiento introduction, and the Georgia Experiment Station's pedigree breeding program refined it into the thick-walled, carmine-red, heart-shaped fruit that defined jarred pimientos and pimiento cheese for most of the twentieth century. Unlike its later nematode-resistant derivative Truhart-NR, the straight Truhart Perfection line carries no built-in resistance to root-knot nematode, so gardeners on sandy, nematode-prone soils should rotate plantings or solarize beds between crops. The blocky, three-lobed fruit ripens from green to deep red with sweet, dense flesh well suited to roasting, canning, and stuffing. Stake or cage plants once fruit loads heavily, and pick at full red color for the richest flavor and color in preserved pimientos.
sources: University of Georgia College of Agriculture Experiment Stations — Truhart Perfection Pimiento

common_name: Aztec Red Flour Corn (Heirloom Red-Kerneled Soft Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep after last frost in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination; Aztec Red descends from Mesoamerican landrace corn grown by indigenous farmers of central Mexico for its deep brick-red kernels and fine, soft-starch flour.

directions: Aztec Red is a Mexican heirloom flour corn grown for medium-sized ears densely packed with glossy, deep-red kernels that grind into a soft, faintly rose-tinted flour used for cornbread, atole, and tortillas. Like other flour corns, its soft, starchy kernels lack the hard glassy layer of flint or dent types, so ears should be harvested promptly once husks dry and finished drying indoors before storage to avoid weather damage and storage mold. It can be eaten fresh in the milk stage as a novelty sweet-adjacent corn, but its real value is as a dry grinding corn once fully mature and cured. Isolate plantings from other corn types by distance or timing if saving pure seed, since open-pollinated corn readily cross-pollinates with neighboring varieties.
sources: The Seed Collection (Australia) — Aztec Red corn variety notes
Native Seeds/SEARCH Seed Catalog

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep and space closely, 8-12 inches apart, to encourage a single unbranched stalk; Rostov is a Russian open-pollinated oilseed cultivar, named for the Rostov-on-Don region, grown for small, high-oil, black-hulled seed rather than the large striped seed of confection sunflowers.

directions: Rostov is a traditional Russian oilseed sunflower bred for a single sturdy stalk topped by one large head up to 10 inches across, densely packed with small black seeds carrying an unusually high oil content compared to snacking types. It matures faster than many oilseed cultivars, typically finishing within about ten to thirteen weeks, which suits it to shorter growing seasons or a late-summer succession planting. Harvest once the back of the head turns from green to yellow-brown and the seeds rattle loosely, then cut the head and hang it to finish curing in a dry, airy, rodent-proof space before threshing. Whole seed can be cold-pressed for oil, roasted for snacking, or offered whole to backyard poultry and wild birds.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Rostov Sunflower

common_name: Chinese Giant Pepper (Extra-Large Thick-Walled Heirloom Bell)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost; Chinese Giant, introduced in the early 1900s, was noted at the time for producing bell fruit roughly twice the size of other bells then available, and it remains one of the largest-fruited open-pollinated sweet peppers grown today.

directions: Chinese Giant is a pre-1900s heirloom sweet pepper prized for its nearly square, extra-large, thick-walled fruit that can reach 4-6 inches long and wide, ripening from dark green to a bright cherry red with mild, sweet, fruity flavor. The compact, 2 to 2.5 foot plants stay relatively short despite the outsized fruit, so working compost into the planting hole and providing steady, even moisture helps size the peppers to their full potential without stressing the plant. Its thick flesh and generous cavity make it an outstanding stuffing pepper, and the large flat surfaces also suit it well to slicing for salads or grilling. Support heavily loaded branches with light staking in windy sites, since the fruit's weight can snap stems on an otherwise sturdy plant.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds

common_name: Pusa Makhmali Okra (IARI Parent Line, Light Green Indian Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm and settled; Pusa Makhmali was released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute from selection within local West Bengal okra germplasm and later served as one of the two parents, crossed with IC-1542, used to breed the widely grown disease-resistant Pusa Sawani.

directions: Pusa Makhmali is an open-pollinated okra selected by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute for smooth, light green pods on tall, productive plants well suited to warm-season cropping. Unlike its own offspring Pusa Sawani, which was specifically bred for resistance, Pusa Makhmali is highly susceptible to yellow vein mosaic virus, a whitefly-transmitted disease that can devastate plantings in regions with heavy vector pressure, so it performs best where okra pests and this virus are not a persistent problem. Pick pods every couple of days at 4-5 inches long, before the ribs toughen, to keep plants setting new fruit through the season. Give plants wide spacing and consistent moisture during flowering and pod set for the heaviest, most tender harvest.
sources: Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) — okra breeding history

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a hanging basket or large container once frost risk has passed; Florida Basket was released in 1981 by the University of Florida's Bradenton research station specifically for basket and container growing.

directions: Florida Basket is a compact, determinate dwarf tomato bred at the University of Florida for hanging baskets and patio containers, needing no staking or caging as its short, self-supporting stems spill gently over the container rim. It sets clusters of small, red, plum-shaped saladette fruit around 2 inches long with good flavor for a container type, ripening over a relatively short, concentrated window typical of determinate dwarf tomatoes. Because container soil dries out quickly, water consistently and feed every couple of weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer to keep the shallow root system productive through the season. Florida Basket later became scientifically significant as one of the two parent cultivars, alongside Ohio 4013-3, used to breed Micro-Tom, the ultra-dwarf tomato now used worldwide as a model organism in plant genetics research.

common_name: Iron Cowpea (Historic USDA Wilt- and Nematode-Resistant Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed; Iron was documented by USDA plant pathologist W. A. Orton in 1903 as one of the first cowpea varieties bred specifically for resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea (Fusarium) wilt.

directions: Iron cowpea is a tall, half-bush heirloom Southern pea with a landmark place in American crop breeding history — one of the earliest cultivars developed with genuine, durable resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea wilt, two soil-borne problems that devastated cowpea plantings across the South before its release in the early 1900s. Its resistance genetics went on to found much of the region's cowpea breeding, most visibly in the blended Iron and Clay mix still grown today as a cover crop and forage, and later in modern resistant releases such as California Blackeye 5. Grown as a food crop, Iron produces good yields of peas suited to fresh shelling or drying, performing reliably on sandy, nematode-prone soils where susceptible varieties decline mid-season. Like other Southern peas it fixes nitrogen as it grows, so it also serves well as a soil-building rotation crop between heavier feeding vegetables.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry — Iron Cowpea, a Variety Resistant to Wilt and Root-Knot (1903)
